bag0: Social Connection and Health: Small Steps Against Loneliness | İhsan Eren
bag1: People with strong social relationships are 50% more likely to survive. How loneliness affects health, surprising research and a small daily idea for connecting.
bag2: Social connection: the forgotten health advice
bag3: According to the World Health Organization, 1 in 6 people worldwide experience loneliness, and loneliness is linked to around 100 deaths every hour. In an analysis combining 148 studies, people with strong social relationships were 50% more likely to survive. The good news: connecting with others doesn't take big steps, and we tend to underestimate the effect of small ones.

bag55: Psychology research shows that we often avoid connecting with others because of mistaken predictions.
bag57: When train passengers were asked to talk to the person next to them, they had a more enjoyable journey than those who kept to themselves, even though they had expected the opposite. The people they talked to enjoyed it too.

bag63: People thought talking on the phone would be awkward; in fact, a voice call created a stronger sense of connection than messaging and took about the same amount of time.
bag64: The power of hugs: In a study in which 404 healthy adults were interviewed every evening for 14 days and then exposed to a common cold virus, those with strong social support and those who hugged more often were slightly better protected against infection; those who did fall ill also had milder symptoms.
bag67: The painful feeling that comes from the gap between the relationships you want and the ones you have. You can feel lonely even in a crowd.
bag69: Objectively having few relationships and little contact. It may affect 1 in 3 older people and 1 in 4 adolescents.
bag70: According to the World Health Organization's 2025 report, loneliness and social isolation increase the risk of stroke, heart disease, diabetes, cognitive decline and early death. In the analysis of 148 studies, the effect of social relationships on the risk of death was comparable to that of well-known risk factors such as smoking and alcohol, and greater than the effect of physical inactivity and obesity.
bag71: For loved ones who can't leave the house
bag72: A stroke, a hip fracture, Parkinson's disease or long-lasting pain can leave a person isolated by confining them to their home and their bed. Loss of mobility and loneliness feed each other.
bag73: Visit or call regularly, and don't keep the conversation only to health.
bag74: Include them in family decisions and everyday tasks; feeling needed matters.
bag75: Hearing or vision problems can lead to withdrawal from social life; get them checked.
bag76: Walking confidently again also makes it easier to go out and meet people. See the guides to recovery after a stroke and after a hip fracture.

bag80: Lessons from the longest study on happiness
bag81: The key message of the study, which has followed hundreds of people from their youth into old age: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.
bag82: Is it living alone or feeling lonely that's harmful?
bag83: Both. Social isolation (few relationships and little contact) and feeling lonely are different things, and both increase health risks. In the analysis of 148 studies, the link with survival was even stronger in studies that measured social relationships in more than one way.
bag85: Messaging builds connection too, but in one study people who talked to old friends on the phone reported feeling more connected than those who wrote to them by email, and, contrary to what they expected, they didn't experience any more awkwardness. If you can, try a voice call or meeting face to face.
bag86: How many friends should I have?
bag87: There is no set number. As Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has been running since 1938, stresses, what matters is the quality of your relationships more than their number: even a few close relationships you can trust are very valuable.
bag88: I've felt lonely and unhappy for a long time. What should I do?
bag89: This feeling is common and it can change. Small steps can help; but if you've had low mood, hopelessness or changes in sleep and appetite for weeks, see a doctor or a mental health professional. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call 112.
